claim: The document titled 'AI 2040: Plan A' alignment roadmap supplement was authored by Ryan Greenblatt and Thomas Larsen.
context:
Alignment Roadmap
Ryan Greenblatt, Thomas Larsen

DISCLAIMER: This supplement is a very rough draft representing in progress thinking.

claim: The alignment roadmap described in this document represents the authors' best guess as of early 2026.
context: This document represents our best guess alignment roadmap as of early 2026. It's focused on outlining high level objectives that need to be accomplished in order to avoid AI takeover.

claim: Preventing AIs from escaping or exfiltrating algorithmic secrets is ranked fourth in importance because it is less direct than backdooring future models.
context: Prevent AIs from escaping, exfilling algo secrets / boosting AI elsewhere. This is much less direct than (1), but could in principle lead to existential catastrophe.

claim: Anthropic has a Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) that includes an AI R&D-4 capability bar.
context: It could trigger before or after the AI R&D-4 bar in Anthropic's RSP (depending on how useful AIs end up being relative to what jobs they can virtually fully automate).

claim: Applying a coefficient of 0.5 to a 100x potential Min-H acceleration yields a 10x safety labor R&D acceleration.
context: This might be modeled by a more aggressive coefficient than 0.6, like maybe 0.5 which only results in 10x safety labor R&D acceleration. This is a large part of why handoff is advantageous at this point.

claim: Plan C in the alignment roadmap refers to a scenario where a basically reasonable AI developer has a small amount of lead time (e.g., a few months) and is willing to take costly safety actions as long as those actions do not cause them to lose the AI race.
context: Second, we'll go over the alignment approach in detail for Plan C, which is the case where we have a basically reasonable AI developer working with a small amount of lead time (e.g. a few months), and are willing to take costly actions that have some safety benefit, as long as this doesn't result in them losing the AI race.

claim: The alignment roadmap described in the document is broken down into 4 phases: Prepare, Mitigate + Elicit, Pause at Min-H, and Handoff.
context:
Our alignment roadmap can be broken down into 4 phases, which we'll discuss in detail:

Prepare. This will centrally involve preparing for control, building misalignment analogies that are as realistic as possible, and various other interventions.

Mitigate + Elicit. During the early intelligence explosion...

Pause at Min-H. Once we've built AI systems with general purpose capabilities sufficient that we can unsafely hand off trust (Min-H)...

Handoff. Once we've mitigated alignment faking and achieved handoff-viability...

claim: Min-H is defined as the level of general purpose AI capabilities sufficient to unsafely hand off trust.
context: Pause at Min-H. Once we've built AI systems with general purpose capabilities sufficient that we can unsafely hand off trust (Min-H), we pause further AI capabilities progress, and try to build AIs that we can safely hand off trust to.

claim: In Plan D, there is substantially less political will, no ability to pause, and much less overall labor for handling misalignment risk compared to Plan C.
context: In Plan D, we have substantially less political will, no ability to pause, and much less overall labor for handling misalignment risk. This means that plan D will accept a much higher risk budget, and focus exclusively on cheap but low assurance techniques.

claim: In Plan B, the alignment approach is very similar to Plan C but with somewhat more time/effort and the ability to spend slightly more resources on more ambitious/higher assurance proposals.
context: In Plan B, the plan is very similar to Plan C, except you have somewhat more time/effort and can spend slightly more resources on more ambitious/higher assurance proposals.

claim: In Plan A, the approach initially plans similarly to Plan B/C to hedge against international coordination breaking down, then shifts resources to moonshots once the regime is stable.
context: In Plan A, we'll initially plan similarly to Plan B/C (in order to hedge against the international coordination breaking down), and then once the regime is stable, shifting resources to moonshots, updating to potentially huge amounts of resources.

claim: The authors estimate that natural schemers account for approximately 3/6 of the expected value of misalignment analogy work, AIs trained to behave like schemers are 1/6 of the value, and abstract analogies are 2/6 of the value.
context: My (low confidence) guess is that natural schemers are 3/6 of the expected value, AIs trained to behave like schemers are 1/6 of the value, and abstract analogies are 2/6 of the value; that said, we're likely to increasingly focus on whichever of these areas ends up seeming most promising (but this isn't very predictable in advance).

claim: Alignment faking in this context refers to AIs being so seriously misaligned that they intentionally fake alignment, such as by scheming against humans.
context: Avoiding alignment faking: AIs aren't so seriously misaligned that they intentionally fake alignment (e.g., they aren't scheming against us).

claim: The document identifies control evaluations, misalignment analogies iteration, and elicitation/handoff viability as core methodologies forming the main empirical feedback loops in the plan.
context:
As part of this, control, misalignment analogies, and elicitation/handoff viability each have core methodologies that form the main empirical feedback loop for that methodology. The methodologies for these are, respectively:

Control evaluations: Control is relatively easy to evaluate because it just requires estimating capabilities.

Misalignment analogies iteration: Ultimately, our main hope for avoiding scheming is probably iterating using misalignment analogies.

claim: Control evaluations are described as relatively easy to evaluate because they primarily require estimating capabilities.
context: Control evaluations: Control is relatively easy to evaluate because it just requires estimating capabilities. This makes iteration easier and control is generally relatively easy to iterate on for reasons we've discussed in prior work.

claim: The Mitigate + Elicit phase lasts from the early intelligence explosion (specifically ITAI) until Min-H.
context: Mitigate + Elicit. During the early intelligence explosion, mitigate the risk of AIs taking catastrophic actions (e.g. staging a rogue internal deployment or backdoor the values of future models). Meanwhile, elicit their capabilities on domains that we care about (e.g. control research, alignment research, security, strategy) and use them to do huge amounts of useful work in these domains. This phase lasts from the early intelligence explosion (specifically ITAI), until Min-H (definitions here).

claim: The main alternative to handoff described in the plan is to stall for more time, primarily by escalating to Plans A or B, which would typically require substantial government involvement.
context: The main alternative to hand off is to instead stall for more time. The main way of doing that would be to escalate to Plans A or B, which would (typically) require substantial government involvement, which may or may not be feasible.

claim: The document's list of research areas excludes some areas such as hardening the world against rogue AIs (e.g., biodefense and cyber defense).
context: This list excludes some areas which receive less focus in this plan but are still important such as hardening the world against rogue AIs (e.g. biodefence and cyber defence).

claim: 'Misalignment analogies' in this context refers to creating and studying AIs analogous to scheming or otherwise misaligned models, sometimes called 'model organisms.'
context: Misalignment analogies: Creating and studying AIs analogous to scheming or otherwise misaligned models (sometimes called "model organisms"). This area will be mostly focused on scheming.

claim: The document identifies 'buying time' as a research area that involves using AI labor to increase the willingness to pay of other actors (centrally the US government and other governments) for lead time.
context: Buying time: Using AI labor to buy time for further safety work. This involves trying to increase the willingness to pay of other actors (centrally the US government and other governments) for lead time, reducing the cost of acquiring lead time for these other actors, and directly acquiring lead time.

claim: The document was published despite being described as a very rough draft, in the spirit of transparency.
context: DISCLAIMER: This supplement is a very rough draft representing in progress thinking. It should be interpreted as internal research notes, not as a final product that we are entirely happy with. This content is dense, full of not-very-well explained jargon, and unpolished. We decided to publish anyway in the spirit of transparency.

context: If we assume that AIs aren't intentionally faking alignment, then their behavior in typical circumstances (and even under some level of generalization) can probably be understood reasonably well using behavioral tests (at least if we're somewhat careful in how we design these tests, including doing things like building analogies for generalization we need).

context: We can also use behavioral tests (likely somewhat different behavioral tests) for ongoing work on elicitation (increasing AI output on safety relevant tasks), though one issue is that this might not be robust to scheming (if the behavioral tests are easy to distinguish from actual usage).

context: We can instead measure AI performance on actual usage (technically this is just a special case of a behavioral test) which might be trickier, but could yield more accurate measurements in addition to potentially being robust to scheming

context: In practice, this plan is somewhat reliant on some version of each of these core methodologies working out, so getting these methodologies to work well (or noticing that they aren't workable) is important.

context: These methodologies are a key part of how we'll achieve some of our main objectives of ensuring control, avoiding scheming, and handoff-viability / eliciting useful labor out of AIs (respectively).

context: Unknown methodology failure: The methodology could fail while we think it actually works. In this case, we can't update our plans based on this failure and instead we're just in trouble (though control and avoiding scheming can act as independent lines of defense).

context: Unknown methodology failure: The methodology could fail while we think it actually works. In this case, we can't update our plans based on this failure and instead we're just in trouble (though control and avoiding scheming can act as independent lines of defense).
